claims.text: Direct solid–liquid coexistence simulations can determine melting temperatures.
Direct solid–liquid coexistence simulations can determine enthalpies of fusion.
Direct solid–liquid coexistence simulations can determine entropies of fusion.
Direct solid–liquid coexistence simulations can determine volume changes at the melting point.
When suitably accurate classical or machine-learned interatomic potentials are used, direct coexistence simulations can provide reliable melting properties.
Using an affordable interatomic potential substantially reduces computational cost relative to full ab initio thermodynamic integration.
The proposed material must have an existing parameterization or training set for a classical or machine-learned potential.
The simulation cell should initially contain solid and liquid phases in contact.
Constant-pressure molecular dynamics over a selected temperature range permits observation of interface behavior and phase stability.
A single classical or machine-learned potential can represent solid and liquid atomic configurations consistently.
Direct simulation of coexisting solid and liquid phases gives the equilibrium melting temperature.
The coexistence method avoids thermodynamic integration performed purely at the DFT level.
Predictive accuracy depends on the reliability of the selected interatomic potential or machine-learned model.
Insufficient training data or inaccurate force fields may degrade predictive accuracy.
A stationary solid–liquid interface can be used to identify the equilibrium melting temperature.
The enthalpy of fusion can be obtained from internal-energy differences between solid and liquid.
The entropy of fusion can be calculated by dividing the enthalpy of fusion by the melting temperature.
The volume change at melting can be obtained from average solid and liquid volumes.
